document.title: Pakistan-Afghanistan Relations
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
document.note: [Confidential] State Department summary of Afghanistan-Pakistan relations and the impact each state has on the other's stability. Covers arms and narco-trafficking effects (lawlessness, arms culture, bombings and assassinations in NWFP), foreign interference from India, Iran, Pakistan and Russia, and U.S. views and policy interests. Says Pakistan lacks a well-conceived end-game for supporting the Taliban and opposing Rabbani.

events.description: Najibullah regime collapsed; Pakistan helped resistance groups agree an interim governing arrangement.
Pakistan convinced nine Afghan parties to accept a government led by Rabbani and Hekmatyar.
Taliban captured Herat; Pakistani embassy in Kabul burned and ambassador beaten; Pakistan expelled Afghan diplomats.
After the Najibullah regime collapsed, Pakistan got Afghan resistance groups to agree to an interim governing arrangement.
Pakistan convinced nine major Afghan parties to accept a government led by Rabbani and Hekmatyar.
Taliban captured Herat; Pakistani embassy in Kabul burned and ambassador beaten by mob; Pakistan expelled Afghan diplomats.
Pakistan proposed sending Foreign Minister Assef Ali and a top intelligence official to Washington for talks on Afghan policy.

key_claims: Pakistan provides material and tactical support to the Taliban but privately does not want them in power in Kabul.
Rabbani believes the Taliban are entirely a tool of Pakistan, while the Taliban have shown independence.
Pakistan lacks a well-conceived end-game and fears a Moscow-Tehran-New Delhi axis backing Rabbani.
Iran, Russia and India are boosting support, including weapons, to the Rabbani government.
The Taliban took Herat in September 1995 and have besieged Kabul since October.
The US supports the UN mission and no particular Afghan faction.
